vignette:
She is 51, European, married, and has spent most of her adult life working as a civil servant. Before the exposure, she thinks of herself as steady, practical, and not especially dramatic. She is the sort of person who keeps folders labeled, pays bills on time, and knows how to stay calm in difficult meetings. Her work gives her satisfaction because it depends on order: documents prepared correctly, procedures followed, risks anticipated. She says that, until a few years ago, she trusted systems. She believed that if something dangerous existed, someone would have checked it.

The event begins as an ordinary workday in a government office building undergoing maintenance. She remembers arriving early, carrying her coffee and reviewing the day's agenda in her head. At first there is only an odd smell, sharp and synthetic, something she assumes is paint or industrial cleaner. Within minutes the odor thickens. Her eyes sting. A pressure builds in her chest, and she notices colleagues looking up from their desks, confused. Someone jokes about the smell, but then another person starts coughing hard. She feels suddenly lightheaded and metallic in the mouth. When she stands, her knees feel unreliable.

What she remembers most clearly is the moment when ordinary office life turns unreal. The corridor fills with people moving too quickly and talking over one another. Someone says not to use the lifts. Someone else says stay where you are. Her throat burns. She cannot tell whether she is breathing enough. She presses a sleeve over her nose and mouth and tries to walk toward the stairs, but the air seems to follow her. Outside, she crouches on the pavement with several coworkers, shivering though it is not cold, and watches emergency vehicles arrive. She tells herself she is lucky to be conscious. Even now, when she recounts this part, she rubs at her sternum as if the tightness is still there.

In the days afterward, she expects to recover once the physical symptoms settle. Instead, the experience keeps returning with an intensity that surprises and embarrasses her. The chemical smell seems to linger everywhere. Cleaning products in supermarkets make her heart race. Fresh paint in a corridor can send her abruptly back to the moment her chest tightened at work. She begins holding her breath when she passes maintenance staff. If she catches even a faint industrial odor, her body reacts before her mind does: pounding heart, nausea, trembling hands, a desperate urge to get outside.

Sleep changes first. She wakes abruptly around three in the morning, convinced something toxic is in the room. At times she sits upright in bed, already panicking before she is fully awake, scanning for a source of danger. Her husband tries to reassure her, but she becomes irritable with him in ways she later regrets. He suggests opening a window or checking the boiler; she hears these as dismissals, as if he does not understand that her body is certain something is wrong. In the morning she feels ashamed and exhausted.

Returning to work is more difficult than she expects. The building itself has become charged with threat. She notices vents, utility cupboards, warning labels, cleaning carts. She studies other people's faces for signs of coughing or dizziness. During meetings she sits nearest the door. If facilities staff mention maintenance, she cannot concentrate on anything else. She starts bringing her own soap, her own hand sanitizer, even her own mug because communal kitchens feel contaminated. Her colleagues know there was an incident, but she senses their lives have moved on. She feels left behind by her own fear.

At work, her usual efficiency gives way to a different kind of vigilance. She rereads health and safety memos repeatedly, not because she is careless but because she cannot stop searching for what was missed. She finds herself drafting emails in her head about ventilation standards and reporting chains. At times she stays late to avoid crowded corridors, then resents being alone in the building. She has become wary of things she once ignored: the hiss of radiators, the smell of photocopier toner, contractors in high-visibility jackets. If an alarm sounds unexpectedly, she startles so violently that she feels foolish afterward.

At home, her world has narrowed. She avoids cinemas, hotels, newly renovated shops, anywhere with unfamiliar air. Holidays now require lengthy research into accommodation, windows, cleaning agents, nearby hospitals. Her husband says she is never fully present; part of her is always assessing exits, airflow, what she would do if she needed to escape. She agrees with him, though hearing it hurts. She misses the version of herself who could enter a building without first imagining contamination.

What troubles her most is not only the fear but the injury to her sense of trust. She used to believe danger announced itself clearly and that competent people would intervene. Now she feels exposed in ordinary spaces. She knows, rationally, that not every odor means harm, not every maintenance notice signals catastrophe. But her body does not accept rational arguments. It remembers burning eyes, confused instructions, the sick realization that invisible air could suddenly become dangerous. Since then, she moves through the world as if safety is provisional, something that can vanish before anyone has time to name what is happening.
